# Structural Engineering Relationships Decision Record

This record initially brought two names together: Structural Engineering Relationships, and Culture-Invariant Relationship Sorting. At the time, they shared only a very narrow starting point for reading the code. The earlier investigation led from the issue name and call name to `UnitsNet/GeneratedCode/Quantities/VolumeFlow.g.cs`, so the first draft identified that file as the main place to look. That entry point is still valid, but the first draft mistook "being able to see the generated quantities first" for "being able to explain the full origin of the relationships".

The original first decision still stands: do not rush to add specialized rules alongside the generated output; first find the callers that actually use Structural Engineering Relationships. The generated file is not irrelevant; it can help confirm that a particular generated quantity is still within the scope of this review. It simply cannot automatically explain where the relationships are created, who consumes them, or whether callers treat relationship order as part of the semantics.

The first draft also left behind a sentence that now seems too broad: relationships "should not swap positions" across cultures. This sentence has not been deleted, because it explains why sorting was later examined separately; however, it is no longer treated as a verified conclusion about the implementation. At the time, there was no stable sample and no complete call result that could distinguish changes in sorting, changes in formatting, and entry-point failures. Collapsing these three things into a single "culture issue" would send subsequent investigation in the wrong direction.

## Limits of the Old Entry Point

`VolumeFlow.g.cs` can still serve as the first stop, for a simple reason: it is the existing generated quantity file, and the earlier investigation records already point here. When opening it, answer only local questions, such as whether the object currently under review still appears in this generated output, or whether the call name can still lead to nearby quantity definitions. The file's location is no longer taken as proof of where the implementation belongs, and the file's public surface is no longer interpreted as the sole source of engineering relationships.

This determined the choice between the two candidate approaches at the time. The first was to treat relationship sorting as an ancillary rule for generated quantities and fix an order near the generated output. It appeared to require only a small change and could quickly stabilize an output observed on one occasion; however, it conflated "who needs this order" with "what the quantity itself is". If another caller needed the same set of relationships but used them differently, later maintainers would have to guess from two locations which order was intended. This approach was therefore not retained as a decision.

The other approach was to review relationship creation and relationship sorting separately. First check which relationships the caller actually obtains, then record what is returned or thrown through that caller's public entry point; assess whether culture affects sorting only through that entry point. This choice did not commit to a specific algorithm or assume a sort key in advance. It merely avoided treating the display layer, generation layer, and consumption layer as a single modification point in the absence of samples from an actual case.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> GeneratedQuantityReview
    GeneratedQuantityReview --> CallerVerification
    CallerVerification --> Structural Engineering Relationships
    CallerVerification --> RelationshipSorting
    Structural Engineering Relationships --> [*]
    RelationshipSorting --> [*]
```

The latter approach was chosen at the time. That decision is still usable, but it is only a decision about the investigation sequence, not an overall account of every way relationships are implemented.

## Boundaries of Structural Engineering Relationships

"Structural Engineering Relationships" is the name of the problem domain here. It is not a module boundary already established from the path, nor should it be described as belonging only to generated code merely because a quantity file appears in the review chain. When fresh case evidence is next available, first find a caller that still uses the relationship, and verify the actual version, entry point, and current result. UNX-208 provides this local navigation path.

The investigation must first distinguish three cases. First, the caller does request Structural Engineering Relationships, and the resulting relationship set or exception can be recorded directly; in this case, the subject is the call path itself, and the generated file is used only to confirm information adjacent to the quantity object. Second, the caller passes through the same quantity object but does not actually read Structural Engineering Relationships; such a sample cannot substitute for the first case, and at most explains why the names are similar. Third, the entry point fails before the relationships are returned; this cannot be classified directly as a relationship error either. Preserve what the entry point actually returns or throws, and wait until the failure location is clear before judging whether it is related to the relationships.

The old draft did not separate these three cases, making it easy to assume that simply opening the generated file completed verification. That understanding no longer applies. The old draft is retained because it did remind us not to modify generated output directly without verification through the caller; it simply did not describe the verification steps in full.

## The Other Side of the Sorting Issue

Discussion of relationship sorting must start with the actual workflow. UNX-211 covers Culture-Invariant Relationship Sorting, so observations should be made only through the public entry point corresponding to that ticket. Do not fold the order in other quantity directories, the display order in test tools, or the declaration order in generated files into the same conclusion.

A convenient shortcut was previously considered: close the issue as long as the order appears unchanged after a single culture switch. This criterion was not adopted. One normal result shows only that the input on that occasion did not reveal a difference; it cannot prove that the relationship sets, relative positions, and entry-point behavior are all the same across cultures. Conversely, one inconsistent result does not necessarily mean that the sorting logic reads the culture: the display text may have changed, the input set may have changed, or the entry point may never have reached the sorting stage.

The retained working sequence is therefore: first hold the relationship input set constant, then obtain results through the same public entry point; after switching cultures, compare the relative positions of the relationships rather than starting by comparing the formatted text on the screen. If the entry point throws anything, record it separately. Exception paths and sorting paths must not be mixed in the record, or someone who later sees different outputs will be unable to tell whether the comparison concerns order or failure.

This does not mean it has been confirmed that the sort key is completely independent of localization. The available material has not confirmed that point, nor is there any need to replace it with a blanket denial. This page decides only that formatted unit names, quantity names, or other display-oriented text should not be treated as the basis for sorting without verification. Whether this substitution occurs must be checked against the inputs and call sites.

## Corrections Prompted by Stale Case Evidence

UNX-208 was later moved from In Progress back to To Do because the available case evidence was stale, and work would resume once a new sample was available. This change explains why the old record should no longer use phrases such as "already reproduced" or "already fixed". The old sample helped locate the starting point for reading the code, but once it became stale, it could no longer support judgments about current behavior.

This also corrects an earlier implicit practice: using the same old sample to explain both Structural Engineering Relationships and sorting across cultures. Both may appear in one investigation, but they are not the same proposition. A new sample must first establish which path it follows: if it actually reads Structural Engineering Relationships, record the call entry point, version in use, and current result; if it concerns only sorting, keep the relationship set unchanged and observe the relative positions before and after switching cultures; if it enters neither path, it cannot be associated with this record merely because the object names are similar.

## Decisions Currently Retained

1. `UnitsNet/GeneratedCode/Quantities/VolumeFlow.g.cs` is a historical starting point for review, not proof of where Structural Engineering Relationships belongs. It helps confirm the generated quantity object and does not replace verification through the caller.
2. Investigation of issues with Structural Engineering Relationships should start with callers that still use it. Without a new sample, do not carry forward status assessments based on stale case evidence.
3. Assess Culture-Invariant Relationship Sorting only within the public workflow covered by UNX-211. Compare relative positions within the same relationship set, not whether the display names are identical.
4. If the public entry point fails, first separate the failure from changes in sorting. A failure cannot be interpreted directly as a sorting issue merely because a culture switch occurred during the same operation.

No decision is made here about which sort key a particular caller must use, or where changes should be made in the generator or runtime code. The two tickets have different local goals: UNX-208 seeks an actual caller that still uses Structural Engineering Relationships; UNX-211 seeks to observe what the existing public entry point actually produces.

## Old Statements Retained in the Margin

> "The generated file is sufficient to first identify where to focus on the relationship issue."

This statement now holds only in the sense of "first finding the relevant quantity object". Using it to skip the caller would mistake a navigation point for a point of responsibility.

> "The order should not change after a culture change."

This expresses the behavior that initially raised concern, not a completed verification. What is needed is a comparison record using the same relationship set and the same public entry point; until such a sample exists, do not elevate this statement into an implementation guarantee.

# Automatic Prefixes and UTF-8 Migration Record

This page remains in the repository because, for a time, people used it to start investigating compatibility issues from the generated quantities file. This entry point is not entirely useless: `UnitsNet/GeneratedCode/Quantities/VolumeFlow.g.cs` is indeed a specific location mentioned in the old investigation records, and you can start here when reading the code to check the adjacency of quantity declarations. The problem is that the old draft turned "you can start looking here" into "both issues should be resolved here", and the latter part should no longer be followed.

The old draft had two migration targets: Auto-Prefix Rejection Rules, and CodeGen UTF-8 Boundaries. It put them into the same sequence of operations, inspecting the generated file first, then replacing the debug entry point with routine calls, and only considering consumer behavior at the end. This sequence was later retained mainly to explain why some old reproduction records left only clues about the generated file, without enough call results.

The following paragraph is the old operational guidance, preserved in its original sense, not a basis for new judgments.

> First open `UnitsNet/GeneratedCode/Quantities/VolumeFlow.g.cs` and confirm that the generated quantities are still present; then switch from the original debug entry point to routine calls. Results related to automatic prefixes are determined by the call's return value, and results related to character boundaries by whether the generated text can still be consumed. If neither side shows any anomalies, the original entry point can be removed. If either side is unclear, immediately restore the original entry point and compare the generated file again.

This paragraph has an easily overlooked assumption: it assumes that "the generated quantities are still present" and "routine calls work" are enough to mean that the migration of both compatibility issues is complete. The initial draft did not record this assumption or separate the material that needed to be retained for each type of behavior. As a result, the same rollback action was used for two different questions: whether prefix rejection was exposed through actual calls, and whether the post-upgrade character boundaries were reproduced in the maintainer's usual steps.

## Where It Started at the Time

The old investigation selected `VolumeFlow.g.cs` not because it had already been confirmed to implement prefix rejection or character handling, but because the issue names and call names had led readers there. The file is a suitable starting point for reading the code: it belongs to the existing generated quantities module and lets readers check the local declarations first, then decide whether to continue investigating the calling side. The old draft stretched this navigational value into a claim about the cause, making later records read as though "as long as the file has not changed, there is no compatibility issue".

This expanded conclusion has been discarded. It is retained so that anyone taking over old reproductions understands that "look at VolumeFlow first" in the early notes is a hint about where to look, not a root-cause conclusion, nor a reason to require all subsequent checks to be crammed into the same file.

The initial draft also used an overly convenient distinction: automatic prefix issues were described as naming issues in generated code, and UTF-8 boundaries as an issue with reading generated text. This made it easy to remember during investigation, but it did not explain where the return values of actual calls, raw diagnostics, and consumer behavior each fit. That distinction was not rewritten into a new, complete explanation; the old page should only be treated as an investigation starting point that was once effective.

## Gaps Left by the Old Migration Sequence

For automatic prefixes, the old steps required switching from the debug entry point to users' routine calls. The original intent was to avoid checking the rules only through an entry point that made observation convenient, without seeing the results in actual use. Yet the old draft did not specify the minimum material to retain: the return value, the raw diagnostics, or both. Later records still show one unconfirmed point on this side, so the switch itself cannot be treated as a verification result.

An old conclusion that says only "debug entry point OK, routine entry point OK" is not enough to reconstruct what the caller actually saw when rejection occurred. If the return value was not saved, the raw diagnostics should at least be available; if neither is available, the page can only record a gap, and declarations in the generated file cannot substitute for them.

The gap in the UTF-8 section is different. The old draft treated "the text can still be consumed" as the completion condition, but did not state which observations from the maintainer's routine steps should be retained, nor did it provide a separate boundary record. The follow-up card required checking by following the routine steps and leaving the parts without evidence blank. It indicated the direction for verification, but did not provide a unified procedure that could retroactively fill in the old workflow.

So the old idea of "migrating both issues together" was not a repeatable definition of a migration batch. It simply put two items to investigate in the same note and reused the same navigation route to the generated file. Treating it as a sign that the combined migration was complete would conceal the lack of material for one of the items.

## The Old Path and Separate Verification Tracks

```text
Old record
Issue name/call name -> VolumeFlow.g.cs -> Generated quantity declarations -> Switch from the debug entry point to routine calls
                                              \-> Any point unclear -> Restore the debug entry point

Separate verification tracks
Auto-Prefix Rejection Rules -> Routine calls -> Return value or raw diagnostics
CodeGen UTF-8 Boundaries -> Maintainer's routine steps -> Character-boundary observations
```

Here, "separate" only means that the paths for retaining material differ, not that new parts of the implementation have been identified as responsible for the two issues. The generated file can still be a starting point, but the prefix track must return to actual calls, and the character track to the maintainer's usual steps. The two consumer observations should not be compressed into a single phrase, "the generated text is normal".

The old migration-batch record has another practical consequence: it described the new path as a replacement for the debug entry point, but did not explain what should be saved side by side during the switch. As a result, looking back at the page later reveals only that an entry-point switch occurred, not which call corresponded to which type of behavior. Restoring the old path means restoring the original debug entry point and the original observation method; this does not merge the two items again, but keeps comparable reference points for the old and new records.

## Clues Left by Follow-up Verification

UNX-220 records that Auto-Prefix Rejection Rules previously exposed an issue through the old call. It still has one unconfirmed point in the follow-up work, which is connected to the initial draft's lack of material from routine calls. This card is useful for recovering the working context, but should not be used to fabricate a return value or raw diagnostics for the old page that were not saved. If the procedure is rerun, the records should follow the routine calls directly, rather than just point to the location of `VolumeFlow.g.cs`.

UNX-225 records the post-upgrade regression in CodeGen UTF-8 Boundaries. It requires checks using the repository maintainer's routine steps, with any parts lacking sufficient evidence explicitly left blank. This requirement makes the old draft's claim that "it is enough for the generated text to be readable" even less sound, but does not provide independent boundary results that can be backfilled into the initial draft. The gaps must still be left empty here, rather than presenting the direction of the checks as observations already made.

The two cards point to different verification actions: the former is concerned with whether the rules are exposed through routine calls, while the latter is concerned with whether the post-upgrade boundaries appear in the maintenance workflow. They can serve as parallel navigation references, but should no longer be described as the same generated-file migration. For another set of checks involving the main library or Modular production builds, see DOC-20; probe issues are not included in this page's prefix and character records.

## Old Recovery Steps That Can Still Be Followed

If anyone is rerunning this migration record, first treat `VolumeFlow.g.cs` as a starting point for reading and confirm that you are still looking at the generated quantities module; then separately retain the routine-call results for automatic prefixes and the actual observations of UTF-8 boundaries during the maintenance steps. If either set of material is missing, do not continue using the old draft's "migration complete" wording.

When the old path needs to be restored, first restore the original debug entry point, then create comparison records again using the original observation method. See what return values or raw diagnostics routine calls can provide on one side, while retaining the blanks where character-boundary checks have no evidence on the other. Do not use the rollback to the old entry point as a reason to mark unconfirmed items as resolved.

The old draft once recommended removing the original entry point after both sides "appear to have no anomalies". This recommendation has been discarded, because "no anomalies" did not specify which calls produced that observation or whether the character boundaries had been checked independently. The page retains this recommendation to identify why the old records lost their basis for comparison after the entry point was removed. If the entry point is still to be removed in a new rerun, it must at least be possible to state what was retained for each of the two verification tracks.

"Migration batch" on this page must also be understood only in the old sense: one entry-point switch, one look back at the generated file, and one observation of consumer behavior were grouped together. It has no batch number and no fixed format for saving call results. Adding the cards' handling status or later verification actions to this old batch would make the chronology look more complete than the original record, and would therefore no longer reflect the history this page preserves.

## Side Notes That Were Not Split Out

- The routine-call material for Auto-Prefix Rejection Rules should still be stored separately from the debug-entry-point material; the old draft did not specify a storage format.
- CodeGen UTF-8 Boundaries still lacks a record documenting the maintainer's usual steps; no assumed steps are added here.
- `VolumeFlow.g.cs` can continue to serve as an old navigation clue, but no longer serves as a common basis for causal attribution.
- If verification extends to production builds of the main library or Modular, go to DOC-20, and do not add another set of build assessments to this page.
- The unconfirmed point in UNX-220 cannot be answered by a file path; the blanks in UNX-225 cannot be answered by the four words "text can be consumed" either.

The historical value of this migration record lies in preserving a mistaken simplification: treating the same code-navigation route as the common endpoint for two compatibility checks. Later addenda only marked where observations were missing in the old sequence, without turning it into a new authoritative procedure. If the page is edited again, this old guidance and the traces of its rejection must still be retained.

Record first: the abbreviation API is concerned with whether the caller can obtain a stable unit abbreviation through `UnitInfo`; Partial Unit System Configuration is concerned with whether the selection scope is coherent across generation, configuration, and examples. The former's unstable output cannot be directly attributed to the latter omitting a unit system. The latter's example result being inconsistent with the entry point likewise cannot be used to redefine what the abbreviation API means.

## Approaches Compared at the Time

**Combine the two issues into a single generator change.**

The advantage of this approach is that the change is concentrated, and review only needs to focus on the entry point for generated quantities. But it ties together two boundaries that have not yet been clarified: the API output contract would be driven by configuration examples, while the configuration's selection rules could in turn easily be obscured by a single abbreviation change. If a regression appears, the result would not show whether the deviation came from the API itself, the configuration entry point, or the example wording.

**Let the examples define all behavior first.**

Examples are suitable for exposing differences visible to users, but not for carrying the API semantics on their own. In particular, the phrase "partial unit systems" does not itself specify which units should be retained, which relationships should be retained, or who should handle an unavailable abbreviation. Using the examples as the sole basis would mean repeatedly rewriting the existing interpretation of the API whenever configuration is expanded later.

**Split the decisions and retain a shared verification entry point.**

Adopt this approach. The two topics are closed out separately, with a checkable conclusion for each; they return to the same location only when confirming the adjacency relationship in the generation code. This does not reduce the amount of work, but it prevents one surface-level match from masking the other problem.

## Decision

1. `UnitInfo` The abbreviation API follows its own public semantics. During review, state first what the caller obtains, rather than inferring what the API should return from an example using a particular unit system. If the same unit behaves inconsistently along different paths, first record which entry points differ, then decide whether it is an API implementation issue.

2. Handle Partial Unit System Configuration based on the selection boundary. Configuration, generated quantities, and examples must all account for the same set of selected units; any phenomenon that "looks like one unit is missing" must not be logged directly as a generator defect before the entry point is checked.

3. `CodeGen/Generators/UnitsNetGen/QuantityGenerator.cs` is retained as the code-reading entry point for this pass. It can help trace local declarations and adjacency relationships related to generated quantities, but the issue name or call name pointing to this file does not justify presuming that this is the sole implementation location. When determining the actual relationship, use the references visible in that revision.

4. The acceptance artifacts for the two tracks are stored separately. The abbreviation track stores the minimal call that reproduces the output discrepancy; the configuration track stores the mapping between the selected scope and the example result. Do not use one combined screenshot to claim that both issues are closed.

This decision deliberately does not fill in complete configuration syntax for "partial unit systems," nor does it specify the exception form for the abbreviation API when a unit is not found. The existing material is insufficient to make these details rc1 commitments; forcing them in would only turn assumptions still under discussion into API.

## Boundaries After Review

The most likely misreading during review is to treat the generator file as the API contract itself. The generator is a valid trace-back point, but API stability still needs to be judged from the call result and the generated quantities API; configuration validity also requires checking whether the selected scope can be explained by the same artifact. The two checks can share code reading, but not conclusions.

Another misreading is to treat "abbreviations cannot be reproduced consistently" as temporary example noise. The phenomenon only shows that the observations so far are insufficient to support a stable conclusion; it does not mean the issue has been narrowed to any one of formatting, caching, or unit-system selection. Therefore, when revising, retain the original minimal call and the configuration snippet used at the time, rather than leaving only a "fixed" note.

For the configuration track, it is acceptable to support one explicit subset first and expand to other subsets later; it is not acceptable to design the entry point from the outset on the premise that "all unit systems are equivalent." This will increase example maintenance, but it keeps changes caused by adding a unit system within a reviewable scope. If an example needs to change, the change description must identify whether it corrects the selection scope, the generated result, or the abbreviation display. The three are not interchangeable.

Further reading can start from the generator path above. If the reference relationships show that the abbreviation API or configuration selection is actually handled elsewhere, add a new entry point under the respective issue; do not go back and merge the two issues into a single broad generator change.

# Global Default Configuration Release Proposal

The interface review starts by treating "Global Default Configuration Release" as a separate entry point. The existing user flow can use the global default configuration, but who reads it after publication and when the input fields are finalized remain unresolved.

There are three preliminary options:

- Publish a shared default configuration for callers to use when they do not explicitly supply a configuration;
- Have callers continue constructing their own configurations, and only fill in the gaps in the existing user flow;
- Settle the input fields first and defer publication to a later interface change.

The first option can reduce repeated setup for callers, but would need to define what happens when setup is repeated and whether existing callers can still keep their own configuration. The second is a smaller change, but cannot provide unified defaults. The third carries the least risk, but would split the interface review into two rounds.

We do not assume that the global default will override configuration already supplied by a caller, or that a single publish operation will change all previously created use sites. Both depend on the input fields and read timing; at this stage, they can only be treated as interface questions that still need confirmation. If publishing is mixed in with ordinary configuration construction, callers also won't be able to tell whether they are merely creating a configuration or changing the source of defaults for other use sites.

The recommendation is to first list the input fields, the scope in which defaults take effect, and how repeated publication is handled, then decide whether to expose a shared default configuration. The current reference point is `UnitsNet/GeneratedCode/Quantities/VolumeFlow.g.cs`; this file can be used to check the local declarations for the generated count and the adjacent code, but it is not a direct substitute for weighing interface trade-offs.

# Global Default Configuration Release Proposal

At first, this looked like simply putting a default configuration on an existing user path. The subsequent review separated the issues: the configuration itself, the publishing operation, and when callers read it are not all determined by the same interface. If we focus only on "the existing path works," it is easy to mistake a caller's current success for evidence that the defaults already have stable boundaries.

The judgment retained in the initial draft was to try sharing the default configuration first, then fill in the details based on caller feedback. At the time, the input fields were not listed separately, and the draft did not clearly state what a second publication should do. This judgment has not been removed, because it explains why later reviews kept getting stuck on the interface shape rather than on the implementation of generated quantities.

## Scope Retained After Review

This round does not consolidate all configuration entry points. The discussion is limited to publishing the global default configuration: after a configuration enters through the public interface, which use sites that have not explicitly provided configuration can read it; whether use sites that explicitly provide configuration continue to use their own values; and whether repeated publishing is allowed to change the results of subsequent reads.

Here, "global" refers to the defaults provided by this interface, not a requirement for all quantity types to share the same internal state. `UnitsNet/GeneratedCode/Quantities/VolumeFlow.g.cs` is still retained as a code reference point: it can help check declarations and call names around the generated quantities, but it does not give the name of the publishing entry point, nor should it be used to conclude that the generated file is where the configuration belongs.

The review also confirmed one point: the existing user path supports Global Default Configuration Release. This only shows that the path already exists; it cannot replace a contract for the fields, override relationships, and repeated calls. The earlier wording that conflated these two layers has been replaced with the candidate options below.

Out-of-scope matters should also be set apart first. This proposal does not decide how each quantity type stores its configuration, does not turn generated quantity files into the default configuration entry point, and does not require all existing construction methods to migrate. The value of the publishing interface is that it gives use sites without explicit configuration an identifiable source; it does not need to use the word "global" to take over local choices that callers have already explicitly expressed.

Another boundary that is easy to confuse is the one between objects and values. A configuration object can hold fields and values, but constructing the object does not automatically mean it has entered the default path. If construction and publishing are not distinguished, callers cannot tell from ordinary object creation whether it will affect other use sites; if the two are separate, the interface must explain when publishing occurs and under what conditions subsequent reads enter the default path. This is why the two concepts are retained in this round, not an assumption about internal storage.

## Candidate Options

### A: Publish Shared Defaults

The public interface accepts a configuration and uses it as the default source for subsequent calls without explicit configuration. If callers provide their own configuration, the caller-provided values still take precedence. This direction matches the expectation of a "global default" and makes it easier to reduce repeated setup along existing user paths.

The costs center on the semantics after publishing: does a second publication override the first, get rejected, or affect only use sites created afterward? Without a clear answer, different callers will naturally make different assumptions. In particular, when an existing use site has already read the defaults, the word "global" alone does not justify assuming that it will follow the new values.

This option also requires the interface to distinguish between "no configuration provided" and "a configuration with default-valued fields provided." If these two states are merged at the input boundary, callers cannot tell whether they are adopting platform defaults or explicitly requesting the same values.

A also cannot commit in advance to whether published values are obtained at read time, obtained when a use site is created, or fixed at some earlier boundary. These three interpretations affect behavior after repeated publishing, as well as whether callers can safely switch from providing local configuration to omitting it. Until the fields are confirmed, there is no basis for documenting any one of these as existing behavior guaranteed for compatibility.

### B: Retain Only Caller-Side Construction

Callers continue to construct configuration themselves, and the current user path only passes it along. This avoids issues with shared state and repeated publishing, and keeps the meaning of the fields more concentrated on the caller side.

The drawback is that every caller must decide on the defaults. Once callers implement different omission rules, the same names can correspond to different actual configurations. This also does not provide the unified entry point that the interface review originally sought; it merely pushes the decision back to each use site.

B has the lowest migration cost, because existing callers do not need to wait for the publishing semantics to stabilize; however, it also means that "Global Default Configuration Release" remains only a convention within the user path, rather than a public entry point. If rc1 takes this direction, it should be described as preserving the status quo, and consumers should not be led to believe that they can later obtain the same behavior simply by removing local construction.

### C: Freeze the Input Fields First, Do Not Publish Yet

Treat the input fields and their defaults as the initial deliverable of the interface review, leaving the publishing operation for later adjustments. This makes it possible to first determine whether the fields are sufficient to describe the existing user path, then decide whether shared defaults are necessary.

This direction has the lowest cost to reverse, but leaves consumers continuing to use their own construction methods. If rc1 needs an explicit global entry point, this option can only be transitional and cannot be documented as a final commitment to publishing.

C is not simply postponing the problem. It first requires the review to distinguish which fields are explicitly supplied by callers, which fields may be filled in from a default source, and whether a missing field is truly equivalent to the caller choosing the default value. As long as these judgments remain conflated in a single input state, even adding a publishing operation later will not explain the boundary between explicit configuration and no configuration.

## Recommendation for This Round

Prepare the interface along the lines of A, but do not expose the publishing operation before the fields are confirmed. The reason is not that shared defaults are inherently infeasible, but that the fields determine whether the defaults can be interpreted consistently. Fix the fields first, then confirm three behaviors:

1. Whether calls that do not explicitly provide configuration read the published values;
2. Whether explicit configuration always overrides the published values;
3. When publishing again within the same process, what existing use sites and subsequent use sites each see.

These three items are not a substitute for a test list; they are semantic boundaries that must be documented for the interface. If any one of them can only be answered by relying on implementation details, this should not be published as a public default configuration.

For callers, the most important point is not to interpret "default" as necessarily overriding other values. When callers already have their own configuration, they should still be able to express that fact; only callers without configuration should enter the shared-default path. This preserves the current user path without requiring every caller to guess whether global configuration has already been set.

After the fields are finalized, the review should also separately check whether callers that omit local configuration would lose distinctions they could previously express. This does not require immediate changes to existing callers; first establish whether they are intentionally passing local values or merely repeating values that a default source could provide. These two cases cannot be handled by the same migration. The former must retain a local entry point, while only the latter may choose to adopt shared defaults once the publishing semantics are clear.

The publishing operation should not be described as a one-time, irreversible initialization either. If a second publication is to be allowed in the future, the interface must document the read boundaries it affects; if it is not allowed, the rejection conditions must be exposed directly to callers. Relying solely on call order would make results within the same process incidental, which neither helps callers reason about them nor provides a stable commitment for rc1.

## Disagreements During Review

The disagreement is not about whether defaults are needed, but whether the publishing operation is part of the configuration object. One view is that constructing a configuration should also determine whether it becomes the global default; the other is that construction and publishing must be separate, to prevent ordinary object creation from unexpectedly affecting other callers.

The former makes calls shorter, but when a failure occurs, it is difficult to tell whether the problem lies in the fields or the publishing timing. The latter requires more steps, but lets callers explicitly choose the scope of the effect. The current preference is to retain separate concepts: the configuration object describes the values, and the publishing operation describes when it enters the default path. The exact shape of API has not yet been finalized.

Another old assumption needs correction: the initial draft assumed that a second publication could directly override the first. Later checks found no interface contract supporting this, so overriding cannot be treated as existing behavior. At the interface level, a second publication must be explicitly defined as one of three things: overriding, being rejected, or affecting only subsequent reads; until then, the related usage patterns remain candidates, not compatibility commitments.

The review also included the view that "the existing user path already works, so publishing semantics do not need to be specified separately." This view can explain the status quo, but is insufficient to determine the public interface. The fact that a user path can bring configuration to the current use site does not answer when another use site may omit configuration, nor does it answer which caller should see which value when two callers publish in sequence. Leaving these questions to the implementation would instead expand originally local differences between paths into differences between callers.

## Verification Entry Points Before Publishing

UNX-214 records the evidence to retain for the automation entry point: the corresponding job must be triggered through the repository's existing automation entry point, and the job, commit, and actual artifact name must be recorded. This evidence is used to confirm whether the publishing path went through the expected job, not as a substitute for judgments about interface semantics.

The card later entered risk review. It was subsequently blocked because the upstream interface owner had not yet confirmed the input fields. This status is consistent with this proposal: while the fields may still change, there is no point in continuing to discuss override order; even if the implementation is temporarily usable, that is not a basis for fixing the input shape.

This review did not infer publishing behavior from `VolumeFlow.g.cs`. That file is retained only as a local reference point: first check the declarations and adjacent naming around the generated quantities, then return to the actual reference sites to confirm the current user path. The purpose is not to put configuration logic into generated code, but to avoid review judgments based on similar names that refer to different calling surfaces.

The retained automation evidence also has its own boundaries. The job, commit, and actual artifact name can help determine whether this trigger followed the expected publishing path; they cannot replace conclusions about field meanings, explicit overrides, or repeated publishing. Even a completed job only shows that this path was executed, not that all callers will read the default configuration in the same way.

## Withdrawal Conditions

If the fields cannot distinguish between no configuration and explicit configuration, withdraw A and use C first. If the behavior of repeated publishing can only be determined by the internal initialization order, withdraw A as well; the publishing interface must not leave timing questions for callers to guess.

If the existing user path already covers the target usage patterns without introducing shared defaults, B remains a conservative fallback for rc1. However, when choosing B, make it clear that it does not provide a unified publishing capability; "it works today" cannot substitute for this distinction.

If the review can only explain read results after the first publication, but cannot explain any of the options for a second publication, rejecting a second publication, or limiting its scope of effect, A should not enter rc1 either. At that point, adding a vague sentence will not reduce the risk; instead, return to C and first fix an acceptable input shape. Once the fields and read boundaries can each be explained separately, compare the costs of shared defaults and caller-side construction again.

Items awaiting confirmation: the final set of input fields; the contract for repeated publishing; whether existing callers have local configuration behavior that must be preserved. After the fields are confirmed, decide whether the publishing operation will be included in rc1.

# Name-Based Abbreviation Lookup Investigation Notes

The case encountered during rc1 wasn't simply a missing abbreviation: the input looked like a unit name, but the query didn't resolve to the expected default abbreviation. The old notes first attributed this class of issue to the generated quantity-name table; only later did it become clear that names, units, and abbreviations couldn't be looked up interchangeably here.

First, save the input from the incident. Don't start by replacing the name with an abbreviation, or swap parameters just because the quantity name and unit name are similar. Capitalization, spaces, plural forms, and parameter positions in the original input can all change which branch is taken. If the caller has already normalized the name, the only option is to compare the values before and after normalization; with only the latter, you won't be able to tell later whether the entry point changed the term or the quantity data never contained it.

Start the investigation at `CodeGen/Generators/UnitsNetGen/QuantityGenerator.cs`. The old notes point here because name information, quantity, unit, names, based, and provides had appeared in the same generation-side neighborhood. This is a useful place to check what name data the generation side made available to queries; it does not by itself establish that values are necessarily read in the same order at runtime.

## Check the outcome first

**The query returns no result**: First, record "quantity name did not match" and "unit name did not match" separately. The old approach treated both as a missing default abbreviation and then added an abbreviation; this often mischaracterized the issue. When a name doesn't match, first check whether the generated set of names contains the original term. When a unit name doesn't match, check whether the term is actually a quantity name, or just display text the caller uses to represent a unit.

**The query returns a unit but no abbreviation**: Check whether the generation side went through the default-abbreviation entry point. The old path showed neighboring names such as `getdefaultabbreviation`. During the investigation, distinguish between "no unit object" and "a unit object exists but its default abbreviation is empty." For the former, go back to name matching; only for the latter does it make sense to inspect the abbreviation data itself. Don't replace an empty string with the name; that would make the display look fixed while changing what the query result means.

**The query ends with an exception**: In the old incident, all exceptions were recorded as `UnitNotFoundException`. That attribution is too broad. First, capture the exception type, the term passed in, and any quantity or unit information already resolved. If no object has been resolved yet, don't record it as an abbreviation-branch failure. Name lookup, unit lookup, and default abbreviation retrieval can each end early; the exception name alone is not enough to locate the failure.

## When names are identical or similar

Name-based queries are especially easy to misread when terms "look the same." A quantity name identifies the quantity, while a unit name identifies the unit; both may have names in the generated material. If a term first matches a quantity and that quantity then supplies its default unit, explicitly record that intermediate result. If a term matches a unit directly, don't override it with the quantity's default unit.

The old recovery procedure suggested this: as long as the object pointed to by `based` exists, follow it as a fallback to retrieve the abbreviation. This action is retained here because it explains some of what was observed at the time, but it is not a reliable basis for a fix. `based` reflects adjacency information in the generated relationships; it does not tell you which unit a name query should fall back to. When you reach this branch, stop at the resolved object and record the name-match and abbreviation-read results separately. Don't keep guessing by automatically following relationships.

Likewise, when you see `provides`, don't immediately conclude that this quantity provides a displayable unit name. The old notes treated it as evidence of name coverage, but later comparisons often established only that a relationship description existed on the generation side. What the query investigation needs is the name that actually matched and the abbreviation returned, not whether a relationship field is present.

## Steps for reproducing from the old notes

1. Use the original term from the incident and copy down the return value or exception without rewriting the input.
2. Determine whether the original term was treated as a quantity or a unit; stop here if neither matched.
3. Once you have a unit, check default abbreviation retrieval. Record an empty value separately from a lookup failure.
4. If the name is long, contains spaces, or differs in capitalization, keep a separate comparison input; don't lump it together with the baseline input as "name not supported."
5. Only if the generation side is actually missing the name or abbreviation data should you return to the area around `QuantityGenerator.cs` to inspect the generation logic further.

This sequence is meant to avoid changing the data first and only later discovering that the entry point passed the wrong term. In the old notes, "name query failed" usually described only the final symptom, without recording the intermediate matched object. So when you encounter the same title again, filling in the intermediate results is more useful than changing the generator first.

## Where to stop

If you can confirm that the original term produces no name match and the generation-side data also has no corresponding name, stop at the finding of missing name data; don't infer anything further about the default abbreviation. If the name match and unit object have both been confirmed, but reading the default abbreviation returns an empty value, stop at the abbreviation-data boundary and don't substitute the name. If all you have is an exception, without the input and intermediate objects, the old notes are insufficient to determine which branch was taken; preserve the exception context and wait for the caller to supply the original parameters.

"Fallback" here is the term used during the investigation at the time; it does not mean all name-based queries should follow the relationship graph to find a substitute unit. Later, someone handled similar cases by filling in abbreviations with names, which conflated missing data with incorrect matches; this reminder remains in the notes to help trace the earlier symptoms.

# History of Logarithmic Arithmetic and Type Conversion

This page preserves a requirements history that was never fully cleaned up. The early investigation listed "Logarithmic Quantity Arithmetic" and "Type-Erased Unit Conversion" side by side, starting not from a verified shared implementation, but from the navigational relationship among issue names, call names, and `CodeGen/Generators/UnitsNetGen/QuantityGenerator.cs`. At the time, the easiest conclusion to write down was "since we have entered the generator directory, both work items must be in the generator". That conclusion was not adopted.

## What to Retain First

The options on record at the time were narrowly scoped:

- Treat `QuantityGenerator.cs` directly as the main thread, and explain both issues through the local declarations;
- Treat it only as a search entry point, follow the references to `v_prev` to confirm the actual invocation, and then document the two issues separately.

The second approach could not provide an end-to-end explanation in the short term, and also required accepting that verification might stop halfway. The decision was to use the second approach. The path was retained because it did carry forward the earlier investigation, and attribution was deferred because there were no actual references, test outputs, or consumer-side results connecting the path to the behavior at the time.

This also limited the scope of the decision at the time: do not change the generator based on a filename, and do not attribute behavior to the runtime merely because runtime appears in the issue description; check references before discussing behavior; separate the two requirements before deciding whether they need a revision in the same location. This decision addressed only documentation and the order of verification, and did not settle where the code should go.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> RecordedSideBySide
    RecordedSideBySide --> PathTraceback
    PathTraceback --> SeparateVerification
    SeparateVerification --> PendingEvidence
```

## Gaps Left by the Initial Draft

v1 did not specify arithmetic rules, input ranges, or result formats. For Type-Erased Unit Conversion, it also did not fill in conversion API, type parameters, or runtime exceptions. These gaps were not replaced with a broad "generator issue to be fixed", but were split into two verification items requiring different entry points: one was to find the actual invocation of Logarithmic Quantity Arithmetic, and the other was to find the invocation used in the most recent report and record the results seen by the consumer.

Thus, seeing `runtime`, `ilogarithmicquantity`, `tunit`, `iarithmeticquantity`, `logarithmic`, `quantities`, `typed`, `interface`, or `arithmetic` near the path only shows that these terms were once used to locate things. They can provide a starting point for reading around the file, but neither an individual term nor a set of keywords can establish a call relationship, much less prove that the two requirements share a piece of generation logic. In particular, even finding `interface`, `arithmetic`, and `quantities` together still does not justify combining type erasure with logarithmic operations.

## The October Recheck Remained Incomplete

On 2025-10-13, UNX-218 captured a baseline record. On 2025-10-14, the test machine used by Quantity Runtime Contracts was occupied by another regression run, and the planned recheck produced no results. This situation shows that the recheck was blocked, but does not show that Type-Erased Unit Conversion had no anomaly, nor does it show that the anomaly occurred in any particular module.

UNX-215 subsequently entered security-side triage. As of 2025-10-17, the card still recorded one unconfirmed point for Logarithmic Quantity Arithmetic, and asked another colleague to rerun it from the same entry point. What can be confirmed here is that verification was incomplete; "unconfirmed" does not establish that the anomaly lies in the generator, the runtime, or the consumer, and a single triage record cannot supply the specific semantics of the arithmetic.

These records added chronological context to the history, but did not overturn the original boundaries. They explain why the page continued to retain the earlier assessment of the path: one recheck was interrupted because the test machine was occupied, and the other still lacked a second result. The cards can serve as navigation aids, but cannot replace actual references, invocation records, or test outputs.

## The Decision That Remains in Place

A shared history page is still maintained, but the two work items are not described as a shared implementation. Logarithmic Quantity Arithmetic and Type-Erased Unit Conversion can be tracked side by side because they belong to the same round of requirements; this side-by-side tracking describes only a relationship in the documentation, not runtime semantics, and does not imply that they need the same fix.

Three statements must be distinguished: an issue name or call name once pointed to `CodeGen/Generators/UnitsNetGen/QuantityGenerator.cs`, which is a navigation fact left by the earlier investigation; that file contains the final implementation, which has not been confirmed; the two issues are resolved by the same piece of generation logic, which has not been confirmed either. The latter two statements cannot be inferred from the first.

If this page is expanded further, new material should connect the entry point to the result: Logarithmic Quantity Arithmetic requires the actual invocation and the path triggered by existing tests or examples; Type-Erased Unit Conversion requires the invocation used in the most recent report and the results seen by the consumer. When all that is available is local declarations or similar keywords, the earlier decision still applies, and no call chain should be filled in. UNX-215 is used to trace back the former, and UNX-218 to trace back the latter; neither card provides a conclusion about the implementation.

## Older Wording That Has Not Yet Been Removed

The page still retains the earlier statement that "the generator directory is the starting point for tracing back", because it explains why the historical records started here. It is not a description of the current implementation, nor can it replace reference checks. Later readers who only need to trace why an issue name led to this file can follow that path; those deciding where to make changes still need to see actual references or test material connecting the entry point, behavior, and results.

Also retained is the fact that the two requirements were once placed on the same page. Being adjacent in the requirements history does not mean being adjacent in the code. Once the test machine becomes available again or another rerun returns results, a local excerpt should be added next to the corresponding issue, explaining which entry point the new evidence covers; until then, the old path, the blocked recheck, and the unconfirmed status should not be polished into definitive conclusions.

## Sequence

|---|---|---|

The guidance left by UNXA-009 is to date the old judgment, then append the new UnitsNet · Performance Lab result side by side. After the user path recovered, the current revision from the second run or read still needs to be backfilled, the relation graph change still needs an explanation, and it is still unknown how many consumers actually read the divergent content. # UnitsNet Performance Lab Incident Postmortem

This page was not originally designed for merging records. It began with an entry-point discrepancy: in the UnitsNet · Performance Lab of adj-unitsnet, the current revisions of two revisions were placed under the same entry point. The entry point could still return content, and the user path was later restored as well, so the anomaly did not manifest as a straightforward total outage; what was truly difficult to determine was which record the entry point had actually pointed to at the time, a question the green results after recovery could not answer.

Only one brief assessment survived from the earliest investigation: the registry identity differed from that of the old record. That version did not include complete timestamps, nor did it reconstruct the pre-failure state. The original text also stated `UnitInfo can recover, why the relation graph changed is still unknown`. This sentence preserves the limits of what was known at the time:`UnitInfo` was the object observed to recover, while the change in the relation graph remained unexplained, not a confirmed cause.

## Incident Window

The entire Performance Lab was not initially classified as affected at the time.`QuantityInfo` remained normal in the comparison, so the investigation was initially narrowed to `UnitInfo` and its entry point. This narrowing was very limited: it could only establish that one read result differed from another, not that all other adopters encountered the same issue, nor that the two revisions had been merged again.

The relative timeline was reconstructed from the few retained records, with its precision still limited to that of the original records:

| Time | Observable facts | How the assessment changed |
|---|---|---|
| T+00 | `UnitsNet-Performance Lab-The two record versions were not merged` first diverged from the old record, with a mismatched registry identity | Started with the entry-point discrepancy, without first attributing it to a specific cause |
| T+07 | `QuantityInfo` was still normal | No longer included all quantity objects in the affected scope |
| T+18 | The comparison shifted to `UnitInfo` | The scope of impact narrowed, while the relationship changes remained unexplained |
| T+31 | The user path was restored | Access recovery and root-cause confirmation were recorded separately |

There is no basis for filling in an absolute start time for this timeline. The actions preserved in later records can only establish the order of these fragments, not that no other operations occurred during each interval. The "Missing timestamp: ____" in the early draft was not retroactively filled in with a seemingly accurate date.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> EntrySplit: Two versions of the record appear at the same entry point
    EntrySplit --> Saved: Preserve the entry-point version
    Saved --> Compared: Compare QuantityInfo and UnitInfo
    Compared --> Narrowed: QuantityInfo is working normally
    Narrowed --> AccessRestored: User path restored
    Narrowed --> EvidenceMissing: Second result still missing
    AccessRestored --> EvidenceMissing
    EvidenceMissing --> Compared: Original input arrives
```

`AccessRestored` in the diagram is not a terminal state. It corresponds only to the restoration of the user path in the timeline; `EvidenceMissing` preserves the fact that the second result for the current revision, the pre-failure entry-point state, and the relation graph changes have not yet been captured in the same original record.

## Traces left by the initial response

After the entry-point discrepancy was noticed, the response was to preserve the version of `docs/adj-unitsnet/incidents/UnitsNet-performance-lab-two-record-versions-not-merged.md` at that time and stop further retries. The retries were stopped not because the root cause had been found, but because the state first needed to be preserved. Without a fixed input, a subsequent successful read can only produce a new result, and cannot reconstruct what the entry point contained at the time of failure.

This trade-off remained valid later on. The earlier account consisting only of a screenshot lacked the original request, revision, and run id. It can show that someone saw the failure screen, but cannot show which revision the screen corresponded to, nor can it explain why another path was working normally. The collated successful result likewise cannot replace that screenshot, much less fill in the missing request context.

Therefore, this incident involved two distinct recovery actions. One was preserving the original state and stopping repeated attempts, and the other was the user path recovering at around T+31. The former preserved an entry point that could be cross-checked, while the latter only changed whether users could continue accessing it. The available material does not establish that a complete record merge took place between the two.

The early records described "current revision" as if it were a stable object. That wording now seems too broad, but it should not be deleted, because it explains why attention was focused on the entry point at the time. A more precise formulation is: the entry point held two records simultaneously at that moment, and the revision on which the second read was based has not been added back. The latter formulation narrows the assessment, without turning historical wording into a current guarantee.

## Why the screenshot did not close out the issue

The screenshot is the piece of evidence most easily overvalued in this postmortem. It preserved a post-failure view, but did not place that view back in the context of the request, revision, and execution location. Without these connections, the screenshot cannot show whether it represents the first or second read, nor establish whether it occurred before or after the entry-point deviation, or after the recovery action.

This does not call for reproducing the same behavior. UNXA-002 already document the handling principle: when the original request associated with the exit entry point has not been attached, do not recreate the original request. The value of retaining the screenshot is that it can still help locate the original archive location; its limitation is that it cannot replace the input itself.

From this perspective, stopping retries was not a passive response. Continuing to retry would produce more successful or failed end states, but would still not establish which entry-point state the old screenshot belonged to. Only new material that can be situated in relation to the revision at the time, the current entry point, and the relative timing can move the issue forward.

## Items that had been incorrectly grouped together

A later review found that the missing result from the second read of the current revision and an expiration action had once been placed near the same card. That expiration action was later confirmed to have been posted to the wrong card and was moved back to its original thread; it was not part of the same incident context as this anomaly. This correction clarified the incident boundaries, but did not provide the raw result of the second read.

The record preserved in UNXA-001 is "Missing result from the second read of the current revision". It supports the need to supply the missing second result, but does not establish why the result is missing. Treating the expiration action mistakenly attached here as the cause would produce a seemingly complete causal chain with no supporting input; now, only the history of the mistaken association between the two is retained.

The attachments to UNXA-002 did not fill this gap either. The historical record explicitly states that only the screenshot remained in the attachments, and the original failure had not yet been obtained. A later addendum further confirmed: without the original request, do not recreate it. Here, "previously blocked" cannot be taken to mean that a technical blocker had already been identified; it describes a pause caused by insufficient archived records.

UNXA-009 addresses a different kind of issue: how old assessments and new results can coexist. It requires adding a date to the old assessment, then appending the new UnitsNet · Performance Lab results side by side. This approach lets readers see the sequence of the registry identity deviation, `QuantityInfo` being normal, the shift in focus to `UnitInfo`, and the recovery of the user path; it did not elevate any individual fragment into a causal attribution for the relation graph.

UNXA-010 Focus on the current state of the entry point before the failure. When adding one earlier frame for the entry point, retain the last verifiable state before the failure, rather than leaving only the final view after the failure. The final view is already from after recovery; the normal state of `QuantityInfo` also pertains to a different object. Neither can replace that pre-failure frame.

## Recovery actions have not erased the impact

The confirmed impact is narrow: two unmerged record versions were present in the same entry point, and read results related to `UnitInfo` deviated from the old record. `QuantityInfo` was normal in one comparison, and the user path recovered later in the timeline. These three points can all be true at the same time, and cannot cancel each other out.

The unconfirmed aspects should also remain separate. The scope of changes to the relation graph has not been tied to specific entry-point states; the revision corresponding to the second missing result has not been filled in; there is no list or count showing how many consumers actually read the divergent content. Recovery of the user path does not answer these questions, and only shows that access through one path was restored later.

Therefore, none of the following claims can replace the current record:

- We cannot say that a particular revision was definitely the one adopted;
- We cannot say that the recovery of `UnitInfo` means the relation graph has recovered;
- We cannot say that `QuantityInfo` being normal means all quantity objects were unaffected;
- We cannot say that the failure in the screenshot belongs to the expiration action mistakenly linked here;
- We cannot say that the two historical records had already been merged when the user path recovered.

These are not abstract caveats, but actual breaks in the connections in the materials for this incident. Each one must be traced back to a revision, an entry-point state, and a point in time before it can be narrowed down further.

## Why the comparison is limited to the current project

The postmortem covers only the UnitsNet · Performance Lab entry point. The main project and adjacent projects each have their own user paths, records, and exit conditions, and this page does not include their states in the scope of impact. `QuantityInfo` and `UnitInfo` are object names already recorded in this comparison; they do not constitute an enumeration of other objects.

The related cards serve only as navigation for this incident's materials: UNXA-001 points to the missing result for the current revision on the second attempt, UNXA-002 points to the archived record before the exit action, UNXA-009 points to the new and old assessments presented side by side, UNXA-010 points to backfilling the record of the pre-failure state. The four cards are not four independent root causes, nor should they be stitched together in card-number order into a single technical workflow.

This boundary also explains why "two revisions at the same entry point" was not expanded to describe the state of the entire UnitsNet. What the current materials confirm is the discrepancy at the adj-unitsnet entry point. Any broader scope of adoption requires additional original excerpts, rather than extrapolation from a single comparison of `UnitInfo` and `QuantityInfo`.

## The actual review sequence

The review starts with `docs/adj-unitsnet/incidents/UnitsNet-performance-lab-two-record-versions-not-merged.md`. First confirm whether the saved entry-point version can still be matched to both revisions; then check whether the original input for the second run or read exists; only then compare the entry-point state with the post-recovery results. This sequence stems from the gaps in the materials for this incident, not from generic troubleshooting steps.

If only a screenshot is found, just retain the screenshot, the location of the card it is attached to and the existing time context. Do not reconstruct the request contents from the screenshot, and do not retroactively attach the post-recovery green read to the time associated with the screenshot. If what is found is a new read, its position relative to the recovery at T+31 still needs to be confirmed, and it cannot automatically be treated as a replacement for the missing second result.

Filling in the last verifiable state before the failure requires going back one slot from the entry point. UNXA-010 already calls out this action separately because the post-failure view is not sufficient to reconstruct the content before the entry-point switch. Once this slot has been filled in, it still needs to be saved separately from the record of the missing second result: the former answers what the entry point was before the failure, while the latter answers which read left no result.

If subsequent materials only show that a particular path succeeded again, this should likewise be recorded only as a new successful read. It cannot retroactively revise the entry-point discrepancy at T+00, cannot prove when the old records were merged, and cannot eliminate the problem with the relation graph. Early versions discussed the recovery of `UnitInfo` together with the unknowns about the relation graph, later versions added a comparison in which `QuantityInfo` was normal, and only afterward was the expiration action on the wrong card ruled out. If only the final sentence, "The user path has been restored", is retained, readers will not see why retries were paused for a time, and may mistakenly believe that the impact had once been fully confirmed.

The old passages are not the current conclusions. They preserve the working judgments made at the time based on limited incident evidence. The new passages only indicate where the scope was narrowed, which associations were withdrawn, and which inputs are still missing. This avoids both sanitizing the old judgments into a narrative that was correct from the start and projecting the later recovery outcome back onto the initial incident state.

In particular, the sentence `UnitInfo can be restored, why the relation graph changed is still unknown` should still be retained with its context. The later finding that `QuantityInfo` was normal changed how the scope of impact was narrowed; the wrong-card correction changed the incident boundaries; restoring the user path changed the observed access behavior. None of the three answered why the relation graph changed.

Only partial conclusions are currently supportable: two revisions once shared one entry point; in one comparison, `QuantityInfo` was normal while `UnitInfo` became the focus of attention; the user path was later restored; the original inputs and relationship changes have still not been fully documented. The root cause confirmation time has not been overwritten by the recovery time.

Compressing them into a single causal chain would make the missing request context look as though it had already been investigated. The unknowns that remain are not blanks kept for form's sake, but places where the corresponding material has yet to arrive.
