# Samples Release Automation Incident Postmortem

What was preserved this time was not an isolated build failure, but different states of the same object at two points in time. Samples · Release Automation's `.github/workflows` triggered a release, the release entered the build queue, the queue produced an artifact version, and the withdrawal window also depended on this release record. During the incident window, the current entry point and the old record did not give the same current revision. The original page, the recovery page, and the unconfirmed causes have not been assembled into a fully explained narrative.

## Preserve the assessment made at the time first

The initial incident note in v1 was just one sentence: the source generator differed from the old record. The version of `docs/adj-samples/incidents/Samples-release-automation-two-states-for-one-object.md` from that time was then saved, further retries were stopped, and the recovery page was kept separately. This did not eliminate the discrepancy, but only prevented new release results from continuing to mix into the original window.

v1 also states that numeric format could be restored, while the change in target framework remained unexplained. Here, "could be restored" comes from partial results in the recovery record and does not mean that the current revision at the two points in time had become consistent again. The earlier assessment that directly attributed the discrepancy to the source generator was later considered premature, but the original assessment was not deleted; it explains why the generation side was examined first at the time, and why the record was not immediately extended to adjacent projects.

## How the incident state changed

| Point in time | What was observed | Actions preserved in the record |
|---|---|---|
| T+00 | `Samples-Release Automation-Same Object Shows Two States` first diverged from the old record, and the current entry point did not match another record | Saved the original input, page, and entry point version |
| T+07 | `QuantityInfo` could still appear normally | Narrowed the scope of impact, without expanding retries further |
| T+18 | The comparison results pointed to `UnitInfo`, and the states in the two places could not simply be treated as results from the same time | Recorded the comparison object and the entry point separately |
| T+31 | The user path recovered, and a new current record appeared after the recovery point | Preserved the recovery page, with the root cause left open |

There is no complete trigger context for the period between T+00 and T+07. Only a few individual objects can now be reviewed, and the missing actions in between cannot be filled in to construct a continuous workflow. T+31 marks the boundary at which the recovery record appeared, not the start of the incident or the point when the root cause was confirmed.

```text
Current entry point ──┐
           ├─ Different current revision values at two points in time ── Preserve the original record
Original record ──┘                         └─ Save the recovery page separately
```

The diagram shows only the two inputs and two destinations actually preserved in this record; it does not attribute the discrepancy to any particular stage.

## The scope of impact did not disappear with the green results

The affected items under observation were Samples · Release Automation's build queue, artifact version records, and withdrawal-window assessments. These records cannot establish that all consumers experienced failures, nor does `QuantityInfo` being normal mean that the entire release was normal. The recovery page only shows that usable results were observed after the recovery point; discrepancies that had already appeared before T+00 still belong to the failure window.

The records before and after recovery also cannot simply be subtracted from one another. When the current entry point changes, the statistics from before and after the change no longer form a single continuous observation. The handling recorded in UNXC-011 was to mark when the current entry point changed and first examine the records before and after the change separately. The narrowing action in UNXC-008 was to take only the first current revision starting from the recovery point, with subsequent aggregates not overwriting the first value for the time being.

The record in UNXC-003 requires checking both the current entry point and the original current revision; if both are missing, leave it unknown. This constraint was not explicitly recorded until the v2 review materials, while v1's "confirmed only as far as the current entry point" is still preserved under the old criteria. It can prevent a green recovery page from replacing missing original values, but it cannot show at which step the change in target framework occurred.

## The mistaken assessment was narrowed, not rewritten as a new conclusion

The initial attribution to the source generator was only a working hypothesis prompted by differences between pages, not a determination supported by complete build logs. Later comparisons of `UnitInfo`, `QuantityInfo`, numeric format, and target framework confirmed only localized behavior. A recovery result for numeric format did not prove that the source generator was the cause; there is still not enough material to explain what happened with target framework.

"Only target framework remains" is not a reliable way to close out the issue either. The current record still needs to distinguish at least three times: when the discrepancy first appeared, when the recovery result appeared, and when the root cause might be pinpointed. There are partial records for the first two, but none for the third. `generated quantity` and `consumer compilation` appeared alongside the incident details in adjacent records, and they are not being stitched together here into an unconfirmed call chain.

A screenshot-only secondhand account was also preserved, but it lacks an account, version, or run id, making it impossible to tell which entry point the screenshot belongs to or to explain why the other path remained normal. A screenshot can help recall what the anomaly looked like, but cannot by itself serve as the basis for judging recovery. The original page and entry point version remain the starting point for this review.

## Handoff trail left during the review

The read-only account needed for the review was still awaiting approval at one point, so some branches were not rerun. Failure to reproduce does not mean it did not happen, nor does it mean it has been ruled out. The review record confirms only as far as the current entry point, and branches that have not been reproduced remain open; this is also why v2 did not fill in an apparently complete intermediate timeline.

The directory once showed an easily misread state: the person on duty could be found in search, but the actual consumer field was still empty. The old exit-action route for UNXC-005 has been deleted, and the pre-change route snapshot has been preserved; maintenance ownership has returned to the actual maintainer, but this did not provide information about the actual consumer. If the original input is obtained again, first preserve the pre-change route and the failure window, then separately record the first current revision after recovery; results from the new entry point cannot rewrite the old window.

# Three Questions for Caller Integration Testing

When a consumer integrates an extension, they usually start with a name, a page of exported material, and an incomplete call sample. The challenge isn't to explain these terms more fully, but to avoid stitching results from different revisions and collection methods into a single integration conclusion. This page fills in the entry point, version, first result, and handoff boundaries based on the questions that were actually recorded later; anything that still can't be confirmed stays next to the original step.

**Where should we start?**

Start at `docs/adj-codegen/faq/CodeGen-client-integration-three-questions-left-by-users.md`. This is where real call samples, adaptation boundaries, and integration feedback for the extension are kept. The main text and attachments are still maintained by CodeGen · Client Integration. If all you have is the title "Three Questions," go back to this path for context first; don't substitute a similarly named location for the path or append fragments from side pages to the sample at hand.

**The page says `latest-known`. Can that be treated as the current revision?**

No. It identifies the existing export entry point; it doesn't mean every same-named object in the export has version information available for comparison. Missing version identifiers were previously found in codegen-client-integration. Until those identifiers are filled in, keep the sample source and revision information for each same-named item separate. UNXD-006 tracks this exact gap. The export page can help locate material, but it cannot replace version information, much less establish from a name that two calls belong to the same round of integration.

**Why keep the first result after a change as a separate record?**

Because it records the first state the consumer encountered after the change. If normal results appear later, they can be appended as new samples, but they must not overwrite the first record. The scope of UNXD-005 is to recover that first result and confirm that it came after the change; it is not to condense all subsequent results into an "overall trend." If the first sample has no revision identifier, that gap must also be recorded as it is.

**What status should be recorded if collection or execution hasn't been confirmed to have taken place?**

Leave it unknown. Unknown means neither success nor failure; it only means the available material does not yet establish that collection or execution actually took place. This status is preserved in UNXD-007. When adding supporting material, record it next to the original step, along with inputs or results that show the process took place. Changing a blank to failure would lead someone later to think a failure had already been observed; changing it to normal is equally unsupported.

**After the collection strategy changes, can results from before and after the exit entry point be compared directly?**

Not directly. The addendum already states that, after the collection strategy changed, results on either side of the exit entry point no longer shared the same basis for comparison. Samples from both sides can still be kept separately, and each should carry its own revision identifier; but their placement in sequence alone is not enough to conclude that the integration improved or worsened. What needs to be recorded here is that the collection method has changed and that the available material is insufficient to draw a conclusion across that change.

**Should the second colleague reorganize the material into another set of steps before trying to reproduce the results?**

Don't reorganize it first. UNXD-008 requires the second colleague to reproduce using only the material already recorded in the cards related to "Three Questions." If inputs, version identifiers, or the first result are missing, mark the gap directly next to the corresponding step. The distinction this preserves is useful: it shows whether the first consumer's samples were incomplete to begin with, or the second person saw different results using the same material. Don't bring in results from an external environment just to fill the blanks.

**What still belongs in this caller record?**

Actual call samples, the extension's adaptation boundaries, and consumer feedback stay here. These have their own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. If further work is needed on the shared interface side, the handoff should include the reproduction entry point, known revision, location of the first result, and unconfirmed items, rather than transferring the caller record along with its entire schedule. The receiving team's ability to continue investigating does not mean this page has reached a judgment on the shared interface.

**What must someone taking over be able to identify, at a minimum, when they open the page?**

At a minimum, they need to find the export path, the sample's revision identifier, and whether the sample is the first result, a later result, or still unconfirmed. Attachments are not excerpted again here; they are still maintained on the project page. If any of these is missing, the person taking over can continue adding samples, but cannot assert on the consumer's behalf that the behavior has been reproduced, has disappeared, or can now be compared with results from before the strategy change.

**Is "Three Questions" now limited to three fixed answers?**

No. The original three starting points were the current entry point, the current revision, and the handoff entry point. The later additions—missing versions, whether collection took place, the conditions for comparing results on either side of the exit entry point, and gaps in reproduction by a second person—all sit under these three. They don't create a separate set of conclusions; they only help consumers put existing material back in the right place.

For field records that remain unresolved, see DOC-43. This page retains only the Q&A consumers need to continue investigating and hand off; related tracking items are UNXD-005, UNXD-006, UNXD-007, and UNXD-008.

# Caller integration testing handoff procedure

When integration testing stalls, first go back to `docs/adj-codegen/runbooks/codegen-client-integration-who-to-contact-when-blocked.md`, record what you're seeing around the entry point in use, then decide whether to hand it off. Stalling here includes no further results, results changing after a rerun, or only a cleaned-up conclusion remaining.

Start by finding the raw records around the earliest failure. If `numeric format`, `target framework`, or `release build` still appear in the records, treat them only as pointers for tracing back, not as causes. If the original input or the first visible result has already been lost, stay at the record-collection stage; don't fill the gaps with the result of a later successful run.

```text
Raw records available?
├─ No: collect records; don't assess the root cause yet
└─ Yes: find the first difference
   ├─ Difference before the entry point in use: continue on the integration testing side
   ├─ Difference still within this project: handle within the project
   └─ Difference crosses a clearly defined interface: record the stopping point, then hand off
```

The raw records must at least capture the entry point used at the time, the location of the original input, and the first result observed. If things already differ before the entry point, don't keep guessing based on terms that appear later; if intermediate records after the entry point don't exist, don't work backward from what was displayed at the end.

Follow only one branch at a time. Seeing `target framework` doesn't necessarily mean it's framework configuration; not seeing `release build` doesn't let you recast it as a generator failure either. If `numeric format` is just a term in an old summary, first go back to the records around the original input and confirm whether it appeared before the first difference.

Reruns can produce new records, but they can't replace the first failing sample. When a new run and an old run disagree, keep them side by side; if the old result wasn't preserved, mark it as unavailable. If the user-visible behavior of a shared interface needs to change, preserve the sample, version clues, and stopping point, then hand off to the owner with the relevant authority.

# Caller-Side Integration Testing Handoff Procedure

The starting point for the integration testing page is still `docs/adj-codegen/runbooks/codegen-client-integration-who-to-contact-when-blocked.md`. If the standard entry point produces no result, page access is denied, a run stops partway through, or rerunning the same input behaves differently, record it as a stopping point first. Do not jump straight from the final displayed result to conclusions about the generator, permissions, or the caller.

The previous version only said to find the early failure records. This version breaks the evidence from the run into three parts: the original input, the first visible result, and a comparable normal-run sample. Do not enter a cause branch in the tree if any of the three is missing. The original input is what was actually used before entering this entry point; the first visible result is the earliest rejection, blank result, pause, or differing output; the normal-run sample is only for finding differences, not for proving that the failed sample should have passed.

```text
No further result from this entry point
│
├─ Original input or first result missing
│  ├─ Do not overwrite the evidence by repeating the same action
│  ├─ Add the input, entry point, and first result
│  └─ Stay in collection
│
├─ Failure record available, but no comparable normal-run sample
│  ├─ Note the sample source
│  ├─ Keep the existing failure record
│  └─ Find a comparable sample first
│
└─ Both types of sample available
   ├─ First difference is before the entry point: continue on the integration testing side
   ├─ Difference is after the entry point but still within this project: handle within the project
   └─ Difference is beyond a clear interface boundary: record the stopping point, then hand off
```

Before comparing, copy down the original input, any version clues visible at the time, and the first result. Use the version clues only to distinguish the original sample from retry samples. A green result after cleanup only shows that the new run passed; it cannot overwrite the old failure.

The old records include one premature retry. The order is now to save the first failed sample before deciding whether to rerun. If the first sample is no longer available, leave that gap in the collection branch rather than recording a later result as recovery. Even if the record contains `numeric format`, `target framework`, or `release build`, first compare the two types of sample to find their first difference.

Limit the comparison to local relationships: whether the inputs are identical, whether they entered through the same entry point, and which side produced the first different result. Change only one condition at a time. If the input, entry point, and environment all change at once, record them separately first; do not combine them into a single cause.

`numeric format` is only a navigation keyword in the old records. If it is the same in the failed and normal-run samples, it is not a confirmed difference. If the first difference happens to appear here, record only the location of the difference; do not write that the format rules have changed. `target framework` likewise only points to a boundary to check; it cannot by itself determine whether to hand off to the caller, handle the case within the project, or hand off at the shared interface. If `release build` is absent from the original record, write only that it is not yet confirmed whether that node was reached.

## Stopping rules for comparison

The two records do not have to look exactly alike, but each must show which entry point it started from. If the failed sample has only the final page while the normal-run sample has only a snippet from mid-run, first fill in the missing context on both sides; these are not two comparable samples. If only the input can be confirmed as identical and the entry point cannot be confirmed, stay in the entry-point branch as well; do not attribute later differences to the caller.

Find the first difference in the order actually visible in the records, not in a call sequence inferred afterward. If a middle segment was not recorded, that gap is the stopping point. Directory names, average results, and output from another run can all help with tracing, but cannot be recorded as intermediate results from this run.

```text
Once the samples are ready
├─ Inputs differ
│  └─ Return to the caller input and sample source
├─ Same input, different entry points
│  └─ Check the entry points first; do not compare later results yet
├─ First difference appears before the entry point
│  └─ Continue on the integration testing side; retain the unknowns beyond the interface
├─ Difference appears after the entry point, still within project scope
│  └─ Append to the original record
├─ Difference is already beyond a clear interface boundary
│  └─ Record the last confirmed point, then hand off
└─ Intermediate records missing
   └─ Return to collection
```

Here, "project scope" means only the input, entry point, index, or resource location that can be directly confirmed in this integration testing work. Seeing a term that looks shared does not mean the interface has been crossed; conversely, a lack of records after the interface does not mean there are no problems within the project. The person handling the case records only the last node they can locate.

If a rerun is needed, first note alongside the old record that the rerun takes place after the first sample has been saved. A rerun that still stops at the same location can serve as a supplementary sample alongside the original; a rerun that turns green or produces a different type of rejection is a new result and cannot overwrite the original stopping point. If one operation replaces the input, entry point, and environment at the same time, keep it as a separate sample and decide afterward whether it can be broken down for comparison.

## Non-author review

UNXD-004 require someone who was not involved in the changes to go through the original steps once. The reviewer does not need to explain the root cause on the original author's behalf, only confirm whether they can reach a stopping point near the one in the original record. If they cannot get there, specify whether they stopped at the input, the entry point, the rejection point, or a gap in the intermediate records; do not just write "cannot reproduce."

```text
Review the original steps
├─ Cannot start the original steps
│  └─ Keep the stopping location; return to collection
├─ Reach the original stopping point, same first result
│  └─ Continue looking for the first difference
├─ Reach a nearby point, different result
│  └─ Save alongside the original as a new sample
└─ The process crosses a clear interface boundary
   └─ State the boundary and end this project's assessment
```

Use the original author's result only for comparison. If the review result differs, there is no need to choose one as the "correct version"; first preserve the differences and the respective entry points. If the reviewer clears the input and switches to another entry point for convenience, the resulting output cannot be recorded retroactively as the result of the original steps.

If the difference is still within CodeGen · Client Integration's own input, index, resource, or entry-point scope, continue appending to the original record. If the difference is already beyond a clear interface boundary, stop explaining behavior beyond that interface and hand over the original sample location, the normal-run sample location, the first difference, and the current stopping point. Do not include unsupported root causes in the handoff notes.

The starting point for whoever takes over is still the original runbook path. For nearby cases, see DOC-43; if the two sets of records do not have comparable inputs, entry points, and first differences, do not merge them into a single issue.

# Caller Integration Testing Handoff Workflow

When integration testing gets stuck, first go back to `docs/adj-codegen/runbooks/codegen-client-integration-who-to-contact-when-blocked.md`. Records around this path may contain only a rejection, a blank result, a run with no follow-up artifacts, or a difference between before and after a rerun. The goal is not to piece together a complete story from them, but to find the last position the current person can confirm: still at CodeGen · Client Integration, already past the interface, or stuck at the exit action.

The earliest version of this page recorded `numeric format`, `target framework`, and `release build` as several lookup terms. Later additions found that the terms themselves cannot determine the branch. The old paragraphs remain because they show where to start looking at the time; new records only correct their role when there is a sample comparison or an entry location.

## Check the tree's entry first

When the current entry has no further result, proceed in the order below. The tree stops at the first point that needs new evidence; do not jump over a gap to guess the next level.

```text
Current entry shows a pause, rejection, or changed result
│
├─ Original input not found
│  ├─ Old record still exists: mark the input as missing
│  └─ Old record also absent: stop at collection; do not rewrite it as the root cause
│
├─ Original input exists, but the first visible result was overwritten by a rerun
│  ├─ Keep the existing rerun result
│  └─ Mark the first failed sample as unavailable and stop comparing
│
├─ First result exists, but there is no comparable normal sample
│  ├─ Record the entry and sample source
│  └─ Do not enter a cause branch before finding a comparable sample
│
└─ Input, first result, and normal sample can all be located
   └─ Continue from the first visible difference
      ├─ Before the entry: verify on the integration-testing side
      ├─ After the entry but before crossing the project interface: continue within the project
      ├─ Clear interface crossed: record the stop point and hand off
      └─ Exit only, with no acknowledgment: leave pending takeover
```

The original input here is the one actually submitted before entering the current entry, not an example organized later. The first visible result is the earliest rejection, blank result, pause, or different output; there is no need to copy the entire invocation process. The normal sample must be comparable near the same entry; if the only available result is a green result from another entry, it is background at most and cannot be used as a branch condition.

A rerun does not restore the old state. Failure records saved before the rerun should remain where they were; if nothing was saved earlier and later only a pass or a different failure can be seen, state that the old sample is unavailable. Do not change the old stop point to recovered just because the new run is cleaner and the result is greener. The new run can serve as a new sample, but it cannot impersonate the original sample.

## How to find the first difference

Place the failed sample and the nearest normal sample side by side, and first check three things: whether the inputs are the same, whether the entries are the same, and which side of the entry the first different result occurred on. Change only one condition per comparison. If the input, entry, and environment were all changed together, split them into several comparisons first; otherwise, maintainers who come later will not know which change caused the result.

```text
Once the samples are comparable
├─ Inputs already differ
│  └─ Return to the caller's inputs and sample sources
├─ Same inputs but different entry points
│  └─ Stay in the entry-point branch, check the entry points first
├─ Same inputs, same entry points, differences already appear before the entry point
│  └─ Continue on the integration-testing side, do not hand off to the shared interface yet
├─ Differences appear after the entry point, but are still within CodeGen · Client Integration
│  └─ Append to the original record within the project
├─ The first difference crosses a clearly defined interface
│  └─ Stop at the interface boundary, prepare to hand off
└─ Intermediate records are missing
   └─ Return to collection, do not work backward from the final display
```

The first difference is determined by the order actually visible in the records, not by a call sequence guessed later. If the final page displays an anomaly, that does not mean every stage before the display was already anomalous. Leave gaps wherever intermediate records are missing; do not fill those gaps with directory names, averaged results or output from another run.

If `numeric format` appears on both sides in the old samples, it is only shared background. Only when the failed and normal records first differ here, can this be recorded as the location of the difference; even then, the handoff notes should only state that the difference first appears here, not that the format rules have changed. When you see `target framework`, first confirm that the inputs and entry points are comparable, then check whether it really is the earliest difference. It cannot by itself point to the caller, the generation process or the runtime side.

When `release build` does not appear, first confirm whether this statement comes from the raw records or a summary compiled later. If the raw records do not include this node, record only that it has not yet been confirmed whether execution reached this point. If the raw records did stop at this node, treat it only as a visible stopping point; to determine whether the build stage caused it, new local records are needed. Terms in old records do not automatically become new failure categories.

## Access failure through the regular entry point

UNXD-003 correspond to access failures through the regular entry point. When you need to reproduce this type of behavior, make one attempt as a non-administrator under the conditions recorded on the card, and leave the location where the denial occurred and the request/run id on the original card. This action is only intended to confirm the behavior seen through the regular entry point, and cannot be used to assess the configuration or determine the final cause on behalf of the permissions owner.

```text
The regular entry point returns a denial
│
├─ No denial location
│  └─ Add the location and request/run id, stop at collection
├─ The denial occurs before the current entry point
│  └─ The integration-testing side checks the entry point and inputs
├─ The denial is still within this project's resource scope
│  └─ Handle within the project, append raw records
├─ The denial crosses a confirmed permissions boundary
│  └─ Attach the stopping point before handing off to the permissions owner
└─ The previous denial can no longer be reproduced
   └─ Preserve the status of the old records, record the new run results separately
```

The location of a denial is more useful than a simple access failure message. At a minimum, it must distinguish between the area before the entry point, inside the current entry point, this project's resource scope, and permission boundaries already crossed. Without a location, a non-admin identity is only a condition for reproducing the issue, not a basis for assigning responsibility. The request/run id is used to return to the same run; if it is missing, mark it as missing, and do not substitute an identifier from another run.

If access through the regular entry point is later restored, keep the original denial. The new result only indicates the new run state, and cannot prove that the cause of the original denial has been confirmed. If the original denial can still be located, compare the two runs side by side; if the original record has been overwritten, state clearly that the original state can no longer be verified, stop there, and do not use the result after access was restored to fill in the gaps.

Do not group denials at the regular entry point and blank results during integration testing under the same label. The former can at least be split into branches based on the denial location, while the latter often requires first locating the initial result. Even if the two phenomena happen to occur during the same period, that does not prove that they originate from the same entry point or the same permission boundary.

## Branches that stay within the project

When a difference is still within the scope of CodeGen · Client Integration's own inputs, indexes, resources, or entry points, do not hand it off prematurely just because the result looks like a shared issue. Continuing within the project also covers two situations: a difference has been observed, but it is not yet clear whether it will cross the interface; or there are too few samples to compare it with normal results for now. In both cases, append to the original record rather than starting a separate entry with a definitive conclusion.

When appending to the record, document each sample's input source, initial result, and first difference from the control separately. Do not collapse samples from different dates into a single reproduced or not reproduced finding. If you later discover that an earlier judgment was mistaken, you can specify in a new record exactly which part does not hold, but do not delete the earlier judgment; it still has value for the troubleshooting sequence used at the time.

Stop project-level handling at the interface boundary. When changing the user-visible behavior of a shared interface is necessary, do not continue making inferences about behavior beyond the interface. The last node the current project can confirm is the handoff point, and the handoff does not need to include an unverified design proposal.

New samples added within the project should be written back near the original runbook path, not kept only in verbal handoffs. If a sample only shows that an input entered the current entry point, record only that; continue along the in-project branch only if the sample shows that the location beyond the entry point is still within the project's resources. Do not mix the later inspection sequence into the first sample just because the same maintainer subsequently checked elsewhere.

## Non-author verification

The purpose of retaining UNXD-004 is to let someone who was not involved in the changes follow the original steps once. Verification is not an endorsement of the entire integration testing chain, and only answers whether it is possible to get from the current entry point to somewhere near the same stopping point as in the original record. Before verification, preserve the original author's sample; do not clean up the inputs or replace the entry point just to make the two results match.

```text
Verification starts
├─ Cannot reach the original stopping point
│  ├─ Specify which step it stopped at
│  └─ Return to the collection or entry-point branch
├─ Reaches the original stopping point, initial result is the same
│  └─ Continue comparing the first difference
├─ Reaches a nearby point, but the initial result differs
│  └─ Keep it side by side as a new sample
└─ Verification has crossed the project interface
   └─ End troubleshooting for this project, record the handoff point
```

When you cannot reach the original stopping point, do not just write that it cannot be reproduced. The stopping point may be at the input, the entry point, permissions, or a gap in the intermediate records. Reaching the same stopping point also does not mean the root cause has been confirmed, only that this review has a comparable result. If the two results differ, preserve the differences first; do not use job title, memory, or a later green result to choose one of them.

If the reviewer did not have the original input from the outset, they are not required to replicate the original author's environment to produce the missing result. Simply record the step in the original procedure where they could not continue. If the review only has access to `target framework` in the summary, but not the corresponding first result, this still constitutes insufficient data collection and should not be escalated into a framework issue.

## Handoff after crossing the interface

The handoff notes should retain only the four local facts needed by the person taking over: where the original sample is, where the most recent normal sample is, where the first difference is, and why the person currently handling the issue cannot continue verification. If no normal sample exists, state that it does not exist; if the interface boundary has not yet been located, return to comparison preparation. Do not include a likely cause attribution in the handoff, and do not lead the person taking over to believe that the project has already confirmed the cause on behalf of the shared side.

You can write: The input and entry point are comparable, the first difference appears after a clearly identified interface, and the current project has no records from after the interface. You can also write: The rejection point at the regular entry point has been retained, the request/run id can be looked up, and permission ownership is still unconfirmed. Both versions hand over the last confirmed point without deciding the technical cause on behalf of the next maintainer.

```text
Before handoff
├─ Can the original input be located?       No → Return to collection
├─ Can the first result be located?     No → Return to collection
├─ Can the normal sample be located?     No → Return to comparison preparation
├─ Has the first difference been documented?   No → Do not hand off yet
└─ The stopping point and destination have been documented
   ├─ Permission boundary: Hand off to the permissions owner
   ├─ After the interface: Stop at the interface boundary
   └─ Still within the project: Continue appending to the original record
```

Handoff does not mean the current project has resolved the issue. It means that the person currently handling the issue cannot verify anything further using the available materials. If the person taking over finds that the samples are not comparable, they can return the record to the collection or comparison branch; this should not be described as their refusal to handle the issue, nor should missing intermediate nodes be filled in through guesswork.

"After the interface" in the handoff text must correspond to a boundary that has already been located, rather than being entered based on whether the result looks like a shared-side issue. If all that can be confirmed is that the rejection occurred within the current entry point, it should still be routed within the project; if all that can be confirmed is that the regular entry point could not start, it should be routed back to the entry point and input. A stopping point recorded this way makes a later handoff easier than a seemingly complete attribution of the cause.

## No acknowledgment at the exit point

Another stopping point may arise when troubleshooting ends: the handoff time has been recorded, but there is no takeover confirmation at the exit point. This stopping point cannot be handled as a technical branch, and the original author, reviewer, or card maintainer must not automatically be treated as the person taking over.

```text
Preparing to exit the current handling process
├─ Only a handoff time, with no takeover confirmation
│  └─ Keep it pending takeover, and retain the original record
├─ Takeover confirmation exists, but the sample or stopping point is missing
│  └─ Return to collection, and proceed only after filling in what is missing
├─ The temporary task has been canceled, with no takeover confirmation
│  └─ Record that the task was canceled, and do not treat it as acknowledgment
└─ Takeover has been confirmed and the materials can be located
   └─ The current branch ends
```

Subsequent records for UNXD-004 included cases where the handoff time had already been recorded, but the takeover field for the exit entry point was still blank. The temporary task later ended because no one was consuming it anymore, and this status only means that the temporary task stopped progressing, not that anyone acknowledged the handoff at the exit entry point, nor does it replace the original stopping point and samples. If the material is still useful for later review, keep it at the original runbook path.

Missing handoff acknowledgment and technical ownership are two separate matters. Permission boundaries remain with the permissions owner; the side that can confirm the interface continues to handle behavior beyond it. Without confirmation of takeover, the status can only remain pending takeover, and an unconfirmed owner must not be assigned just to close the branch.

Canceling the card also does not require deleting the stopping point from the original runbook. The cancellation concerns progress on the temporary task, not a reassessment of the historical run. When someone later reuses the same entry point, they should start with the samples, rejection location, and gaps that are still preserved, rather than interpreting the canceled status as meaning that the old issue does not exist.

## A few terms in the old records

`numeric format`, `target framework`, and `release build` appeared in records at different stages. Their common purpose is to help maintainers find their way back to the old material, not to form a fixed troubleshooting sequence.

If `numeric format` appears only in a summary, first look back to see whether the original input and initial result are available; a summary cannot replace a sample. If `target framework` appears only in text compiled later, first note its source, and do not describe it as a boundary that had already been confirmed at the time. If `release build` appeared only after a particular rerun, you cannot infer retroactively that the earlier failed run had also reached the build node.

Where these terms appear may be the first point of difference, or may simply be shared context. Branch conditions come from two comparable records, not from how familiar the terms are. If maintainers cannot distinguish between the two, they should stop at the comparison branch and record the specific gaps.

The old terms can also help locate the context of the same record: for example, first find the term near the original runbook, then check whether there is an input and an initial result before and after it. But a search hit does not itself constitute a sample, nor can an occurrence of a term in another run be attached to the old run's timeline.

## Completed cards and page stopping points

UNXD-003 later moved from in progress to completed. This only means that work on the card for the regular entry point access failure has ended, and does not fill in the document with that run's rejection location, request/run id, or first difference, nor does the completed status mean that a root cause had already been established for the old incident. When a review is needed, still start from the original runbook path.

DOC-43 preserves the state of an adjacent unresolved incident. It and this page can link to each other, but the rejection location on one card and the unresolved record on another card cannot automatically be pieced together as the same incident. Only when the inputs, entry points, and first differences are all comparable should they be discussed under the same branch; otherwise, keep them separate.

Completion status does not change the handoff rules either. If the original input and first result were not recorded in a comparable form before the card was completed, this gap must still be flagged first during any later review. If a new run after completion produces a different result, save it separately as a new sample; do not write it into the run represented by the completed card.

## Field Appendix

Below is a short form that can be pasted back into the original record before handoff. It is not a cause report, and blank fields should remain blank.

```text
Symptom:
Original input: Locatable / Not locatable
First visible result:
Most recent normal sample: Locatable / Does not exist
First difference:
Current stopping point:
Destination: Within the project / Permission boundary / Beyond a clearly defined interface
Handoff confirmation: Confirmed / Unconfirmed / Temporary task canceled but acceptance not acknowledged
```

For `Symptom`, record a rejection at the normal entry point, a stalled run, or a change in results; do not relabel the symptom as a generator issue. For `First visible result`, record the earliest content observed, rather than substituting the final display. If the `First difference` still cannot be found, write that it cannot be found, and return to collection or preparation for comparison. The `Current stopping point` should state the furthest point confirmed within the current project; there is no need to explain to the next maintainer what happened beyond the boundary.

If the handoff occurs at a permission boundary, include the rejection location and the request/run id; if it occurs at a shared interface boundary, include the locations of both types of samples and the first difference; if work is only continuing within this project, append the new sample to the original runbook rather than creating a separate cross-project conclusion. When there is no handoff confirmation at the exit point, keep `Handoff confirmation` as Unconfirmed, even if the temporary task has already been canceled.

When the "Most recent normal sample" in the appendix cannot be found, do not change it to "No anomalies" just to fill out the form. Does not exist and not located are different states: the former means there is no comparable sample yet, while the latter means a record may exist but cannot currently be returned to. Neither case supports a technical judgment about what happens beyond the handoff interface.

This page has four stopping conditions: when the original input or first result is missing, stop at collection; when there is no comparable normal sample, stop at preparation for comparison; when the difference crosses a clearly defined interface, stop at handoff; when acceptance of the handoff has not been acknowledged, stop at waiting for someone to take over. The current branch ends only when the materials can be located, the boundary can be explained, and the handoff can be confirmed.

# Runtime Observation Window Closeout Checklist

This checklist remains in an old observation window in PerfTests. It covers only cleanup after borrowing the current entry point: retain the final output, remove temporary paths, and return borrowed items before the window ends. Once the environment changes, subsequent records belong to another round and cannot be used to fill in this window's results.

Two lines from the old draft are still worth keeping, but their meaning should not be broadened to fit today's context. "Don't clean up after seeing `QuantityInfo`" was only a reminder to the on-call person at the time to save the output first; it does not mean that name can be used to determine success. "Stop if `quantity catalog` does not appear" was also a stop point for that window and did not cover entry points that might appear later. The old checklist included `UTF-8 boundary` among the items to look for; here it is still treated as a boundary marker to verify alongside the raw output, not as a new release condition.

## Preserve this round's evidence first

1. [ ] Keep the current entry point and this round's commands fixed, and export the first visible output. UNXE-003 requires preserving the state after reaching the entry point, so retain the states from both before and after the failure; do not keep only the cleaned-up green result, and do not switch environments and export later.
2. [ ] Compare the two generation commands and their respective timestamps, and stop at the first divergence. The scope of UNXE-001 ends here: even if similar log lines appear later, they cannot be used to combine the two observations into a single issue. Pause closeout until the first divergence has been located.
3. [ ] If a rerun is needed, keep `perftests-operations-observability`, the current entry point, and the command fixed, changing only the current revision. UNXE-010 records this narrow comparison; if the environment, entry point, or command also changes, the output can only serve as a record of a new round and cannot be used to assess differences in this round.
4. [ ] Verify the correspondence between the final output and the exit action. UNXE-002 requires tracing the exit action back to the actual adj-perftests entry point; neither the filename nor the page color can replace this step. If the actual entry point cannot be found, retain the material already exported and stop.
5. [ ] Export the current runtime observation console and the exit action before the environment changes. UNXE-009 requires archiving these two items before the switch; even if results return to normal after the switch, it no longer counts as a comparison within the same round.

Supplementary notes on sample attachments, exit-action checks, and document review were all added later, but they did not change the sequence above. Cleaning up the temporary environment first often breaks the correspondence between the first visible output and the exit action; that is why the old window required "retaining samples" before rollback.

## Closeout actions

1. [ ] Once the entry point, commands, and first divergence have been captured, remove the temporary paths created solely for this round. Do not expand the test scope before rollback, or use the bypass for other comparisons along the way.
2. [ ] After rollback, confirm that no additional work is being brought in, then record the return time. Here, return refers only to the current entry point borrowed for this round and its temporary paths; it does not mean that routine maintenance arrangements for PerfTests have ended.
3. [ ] If temporary permissions or a bypass were used in this round, remove them first, then check whether the final output can still be matched to the exit action. If the output has been cleaned up, the entry point has changed, or the exit action cannot be reviewed, do not add "returned" to the record; leave the gap in the record.

The old draft listed "final output" alongside "return time" to avoid leaving only a clean state after rollback. This approach is suitable for reviewing that window, but it does not cover every release scenario; nor does it replace other release decisions. Any additional decisions must still go in their own records, not be inferred from this checklist.

## Conditions that require stopping

Stop closeout if any of the following occurs, and retain the state already exported: the current entry point cannot be found; the first divergence between the two commands has not been located; the exit action cannot be mapped to the actual entry point; or temporary diagnostics have changed the state. The last case cannot be overridden by a "success"; mark it as non-comparable and wait for an independent rerun. Continue to use the rollback entry point beside the old checklist for restoration; do not use closeout as an opportunity to adjust the commands or environment.

If only `QuantityInfo` or `quantity catalog` is missing, do not treat the missing name as a basis for a conclusion either. These are checkpoints left by the old observation window and are not enough to show that a new path has completed. If the raw output is still available, you can first record which checkpoint is missing; if the raw output is no longer available, closeout stops here.

Subsequent review added samples, document review, and exit-action checks, but did not prove that the old draft's checkpoints apply to all paths. This page therefore retains the old wording for reviewing the state at that time. To continue looking for entry points, you can find the corresponding records in UNXE-001, UNXE-002, UNXE-003, UNXE-009, and UNXE-010; the comparison record that changes only the current revision is in DOC-45.

# API Preview Entry Point FAQ

This page retains the answers often repeated during the preview entry point migration, not release notes compiled afterward. The line most likely to cause confusion is still in the old record:

> If the preview page opens and the entry point hasn't failed, you can close it.

That line made on-the-spot decisions easier at the time, but treated "the page still opens" and "the migration is covered by the build pipeline" as the same thing. When a candidate path was later withdrawn, the fact that the entry point hadn't failed could not tell us whether the new path or the old one had been withdrawn; it is therefore no longer suitable as the sole basis for closure.

**What can the existing build-release entry point prove now?**

It only proves that the entry point completed its own build and release steps in that run. It can be a starting point for investigation, but it cannot prove that API documentation previews have moved off the old entry point, or replace consumers' checks of the generated output. The old answer's claim that it "tells us most of the story" is retained here to show why some people used it as grounds for approval at the time; that assessment was later corrected based on feedback from the field.

**Who withdraws the candidate path?**

The migration submitter is still responsible for proposing the withdrawal, but cannot leave only a line saying "the entry point passed." The withdrawal note must identify the candidate path and let people still viewing the preview know whether the page entry point has changed. When the build-release entry point has not failed, the release side can continue with its own steps; this does not confirm the preview's source on the migration submitter's behalf.

**When can the release card be closed?**

The threshold still in use is: the release card may only be closed if the main library and the consumer generation pipeline build successfully on a fixed target framework and opposite-case inputs have not regressed. Here, opposite-case inputs are inputs used to confirm that the migration has not turned cases that should be rejected or left unchanged into acceptable results—not another run of the same preview request.

This threshold corrects the old page's closure criteria; it does not automatically fill in all the evidence for the preview migration. In particular, there is still no material that supports a definitive answer to "what if logs from the minimal consumer project are missing?" The gap can be recorded, but do not use an entry point passing in place of those logs.

# Version Freeze Window: Single-Variable Rerun Notes

The recheck still follows the boundaries drawn in the first round. No separate build path was opened. The repository state, call entry point, and target-framework build record for modular-generator remain fixed; only one input condition may change in this round. What this leaves is not a complete build description but a set of adjacent runs that can be revisited.

The role of fixing these three items is narrower than the draft stated. They give the two runs a comparable starting point, but cannot prove that the emergency fix has been confirmed. During the freeze window, a fix, another restoration, and a caller-side change may occur at the same time; when all of these move together, even if a difference appears later, the record cannot show which one to trace it back to.

The draft stated too broadly that "matching build records are enough for a rerun"; that sentence is retained as the judgment made at the time. For a comparison limited to the generation side, it can still serve as a starting point; if the question is whether a fix can enter the freeze window, build records cannot substitute for consumer-side replay material. This distinction was added only after the follow-up check.

The consumer-side material should be retrievable again from the entry point in the record, and it should be clear that the entry point used is connected to this run's fixed state. Without this part, the results of the two runs cannot be written up as showing that the fix was rechecked; they can only be labeled a generation-side comparison. What must be retained here is the original replay material, not a post hoc rewording of the build-side conclusion.

The actual recheck first confirms that the record still points to the same call entry point, then records the target-framework build record and fixed repository state side by side, and only then allows the sole input condition to change. This order prevents an entry-point change from being hidden inside the input change; if the entry point has already changed, any later difference is no longer a single-variable result.

# Restore Image Maintenance Decision Record

Beichen Industrial Software The starting point for this round of discussion was not an attempt to redefine the release process, but the fact that two adjacent activities in restore image maintenance had been grouped together: on one side was the relation-graph entry point already in use, and on the other was a proposal to adjust the maintenance window. The former answers where maintenance starts; the latter attempts to change when maintenance takes place. Both appeared in the same round of work, but they were not the same decision.

The initial record placed the two too close together, making it easy to read as "as long as the rotation changes hands, the maintenance window and release assessment can shift along with it". After review, the original decision was retained, and these relationships were documented separately. The build pool can be handed over to a different person, and the maintenance window can be discussed separately, but neither changes the current release gate.

The approach adopted in this round is as follows: the relation-graph entry point remains the existing entry point for restore image maintenance; the window adjustment was not approved as a replacement for that entry point; rotation handoffs are not grounds for lowering, deferring, or rewriting the release gate. The window proposal was neither removed nor deemed unusable; the materials available at the time simply did not adequately explain what it would cover or miss after replacing the entry point.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[relation-graph entry point] --> B[Current restore image maintenance]
    C[Maintenance window adjustment] --> B
    D[Build pool rotation handoff] --> E[Change in person taking over]
    E --> F[Current release gate unchanged]
    B --> G[Public types and reproducible numerical observations]
    H[Internal layout of generated files] --> I[Troubleshooting clues]
```

The lines in the diagram do not represent an approval sequence. Both relation-graph and the window adjustment touch maintenance work, but only the former continues to serve as the entry point under this decision. The rotation handoff connects only to the change in who takes over; it provides no new conditions for the release gate. The internal layout of generated files likewise stays on the troubleshooting side, and no compatibility conclusions are derived from it.

## Handling the Entry Point and the Window Separately

Retaining the relation-graph entry point does not mean that it describes every situation in image maintenance. It is simply an entry point that can already be reliably located in the existing workflow. During the review, relation call names were traced, and `UnitsNet/GeneratedCode/Quantities/VolumeFlow.g.cs` was examined. This file allowed the checks at the time to trace generated output back to the relevant relations; that does not make it the permanent home of image maintenance, nor does it define the behavior seen by external consumers.

The proposal to adjust the window is different. It concerns maintenance timing and may change handoff arrangements or the times when certain operations are concentrated. The materials did not provide sufficient grounds for treating this timing adjustment as equivalent to replacing the entry point. In particular, they did not explain: whether a window change would retain the trace-back location already provided by the relation-graph entry point, or whether it would leave some part of maintenance without its existing basis for assessment.

Therefore, "retain the entry point" and "defer the window adjustment" are two independent statements. The former is a choice already made; the latter is a proposal for which sufficient justification was not established in this round. Documenting a deferral as a rejection would disguise unanswered questions as risks that have already been ruled out; conversely, presenting retention of the entry point as permanent exclusivity would also exceed what this discussion can support.

At the time, some people understood the maintenance window as a more convenient rotation arrangement. That interpretation was not incorporated into the decision. Rotation arrangements address who takes over build pool maintenance, the window addresses when maintenance is concentrated, and the entry point addresses where troubleshooting or trace-back checks begin. These three things can appear together, but they cannot substitute for one another.

## Rotation Does Not Change the Gate

The meeting materials were explicit about the restriction on rotations: changes to the build pool rotation affect only who takes over, not the current release gate. The phrase "affect only who takes over" is intended to avoid documenting a personnel handoff as a process exception. Maintenance responsibility must remain continuous after a handoff, but the person taking over still faces the original release assessment, not a set of conditions reinterpreted according to whoever is on duty.

This restriction also applies to the window proposal. Even if a decision is made later to adjust the maintenance window, "a more convenient handoff" alone cannot justify moving the gate earlier or relaxing it. Convenient maintenance timing does not automatically provide grounds for proceeding with a release. If the window proposal is to affect release assessment, it must separately identify exactly what it affects, rather than glossing over that through rotation arrangements.

DOC-52 records the build pool rotation transition and handoff. The boundaries between the two documents should be maintained: the handoff record can describe who takes over and how maintenance continuity is maintained; what is retained here is the decision that this handoff must not change the current release gate. If the two documents use different wording in the future, first check whether "who takes over" has been mistakenly written as "how the gate changes".

## Compatibility Criteria

This round did not define compatibility in terms of the arrangement, segmentation, or internal naming of generated output. Compatibility is assessed using public types and reproducible numerical observations. Public types represent the surface that consumers actually depend on; numerical observations confirm that the same surface has not undergone unexplained changes under the same conditions. Both must be retained, and neither can substitute for the other.

Looking only at public types may miss numerical changes; looking at a single numerical observation also cannot establish whether the interface that consumers depend on still exists. The scope approved in the review was precisely the scope for which the existing materials covered both kinds of assessment. Parts not covered are not automatically validated just because generated files appear stable.

Generated files still have practical uses. `VolumeFlow.g.cs` and relation call names can serve as clues for locating the relevant relations, helping reviewers trace back to them; changes in internal layout can also prompt further inspection. But they cannot, on their own, support a conclusion that API is incompatible. Conversely, when public types or numerical behavior show changes that need explanation, the inspection cannot be closed by saying "the generated layout has not changed".

An earlier, rougher formulation treated the location of a generated file as the maintenance entry point, then treated that same location as proof of external compatibility. Following review, this combined formulation is not used. The file path is a local clue encountered during this inspection; relation-graph is the maintenance entry point currently being retained; public types and reproducible numerical observations are the actual basis for assessing compatibility. The three can be related, but they serve different roles.

## Approaches Compared at the Time

| Approach | Conclusion in this round | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Continue using the relation-graph entry point | Retain | Existing maintenance work and trace-back checks can start here, and the current materials support continued use. |
| Adjust the maintenance window and use it as a replacement entry point | Defer | The scope the window would cover after replacement was not explained, and its boundaries were not established. |
| Let the rotation handoff drive changes to the gate | Do not adopt | Rotation changes only who takes over and cannot rewrite the current release gate. |
| Assess compatibility using the internal layout of generated files | Do not adopt | The internal layout can help locate relevant items, but it cannot replace assessment of the public API. |

The table does not classify the window proposal as a failed approach. It is retained here because, if it is proposed again later, merely saying "adjust the window" will not be enough; it must be clear whether the intended change concerns maintenance timing, entry point selection, or release assessment. Mixing all three into one phrase allows decisions of different kinds to borrow one another's rationale during the discussion.

Similarly, this round did not approve an approach of "first inspecting the generated path, then inferring compatibility from the path". That path did help with troubleshooting at the time, and deleting it entirely would lose this historical clue; but elevating it into a contract would allow internal implementation details to obscure the public-facing changes that actually need to be addressed. The filename is retained to record the inspection history, not to broaden its authority.

## Reservations After Review

Two questions about the window adjustment remain unanswered. First, does it affect only day-to-day maintenance arrangements, or would it actually replace the relation-graph entry point? Second, if it is claimed to affect compatibility assessment, what is its direct relationship to public types and reproducible numerical observations? The materials for this round did not answer these questions, so no answers were supplied to fill the gaps.

Another reservation concerns the scope of the evidence. The review approves only the parts covered by existing evidence and does not automatically classify unexamined items based on the existing entry point or the existing generated layout. This restraint does not reject the window or deny the value of generated files in troubleshooting; it simply refuses to expand local clues into a complete release assessment.

If further materials about the window are supplied later, they should first make clear where the proposal belongs: it changes when maintenance takes place, changes the entry point for maintenance, or calls for the release gate to be re-examined. If they only add details about the internal form of generated output, they should still be retained as troubleshooting clues and not rewritten as conclusions about external compatibility.

The current decision remains unchanged: continue using the relation-graph entry point; defer the maintenance window adjustment; the build pool rotation affects only who takes over; the current release gate does not change because of a handoff; compatibility continues to be assessed using public types and reproducible numerical observations.

# Generator Build Pool Transition Handoff

This rotation is not about moving all generator consumers to the new pool at once. The handoff starts with the existing CodeGen consumers: first count all call sites still using the old entry point, then select one consumer that can roll back independently to try the candidate path. The existing call-relationship record is in DOC-01; this preserves the sequence and stop points to hand to the next person on rotation when switching the build pool.

## Pre-handoff inventory

List the known consumers first, with the entry point currently used by each consumer on the same line. Record only call sites that have been confirmed; do not count suspected consumers toward the completed scope. Keep the old entry point in the table as well, because if the candidate path fails, the consumer must be able to switch itself back rather than wait for the build pool to make another full-scale adjustment.

Each row must include at least three things: whether that consumer can roll back independently, where the minimal-consumer reproduction lives, and which artifacts it can access during this switch. The artifact access boundary must be documented clearly to avoid handing changes to the runtime, CodeGen, or Modular to a consumer that can see only part of the output. Do not start the switch until all callers have been counted.

## Candidate path

From the inventoried consumers, choose one with the shortest rollback action and have it switch to the candidate build pool first. Do not bring in a second consumer in the same rotation. That consumer must retain the minimal-consumer reproduction: it should cover the actual consumer compilation entry point, rather than merely showing that the generator project itself builds successfully.

When the reproduction fails, record the failing input and failure location together. The failing input is the consumer-side condition that triggers the problem; do not summarize it as "build failed." The rotation owner uses this to determine whether the problem lies in the runtime, CodeGen, or Modular. After review by the corresponding module owner, decide whether to continue fixing the candidate path or return to the old entry point. Keep the review record with that consumer; do not open a separate generalized conclusion.

## Return to the old entry point

If the candidate path does not pass the minimal-consumer reproduction, or the consumer cannot explain how it can roll back on its own, immediately restore that consumer's old entry point. After restoration, retain the original failing input and artifact access boundary; do not delete this attempt from the handoff table—the next person on rotation needs to know what it tried.

Restoring the old entry point does not mean the build-pool switch is complete. A consumer may be removed from migration only after the known consumers and rollback actions have both been recorded, and the trial consumer has left a module review record. Keep the remaining call sites marked as in migration and schedule them only after they have the conditions for independent rollback.
